clue.text: Assemble around snake biting queen consort

indicators.note: the word for 'assemble' goes around everything that follows it

parts.note: to collate is to gather pages or facts together in order

indicators.note: a snake biting something holds it in its jaws, so the snake holds the queen

parts.note: the boa constrictor, crosswords' favourite snake
R for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A zookeeper gathers round as a snake sinks its fangs into a royal consort.
explanation.walkthrough: BORA goes inside COLLATE, between its A and T. 'Queen consort' reads as one royal title, but 'consort' is split off as the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To consort with people is to keep company and work alongside them, which is close to joining forces in a shared effort.

clue.text: Look after clergyman

definitions.meaning: the verb a museum uses for selecting and caring for a collection
an assistant priest in a parish

explanation.walkthrough: CURATE works both ways: the verb comes from the Latin for care, the same root as the noun for a priest with the cure of souls.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means tending an exhibition or collection; the noun is a junior parish priest in the Church of England.

clue.text: Latecomer dancing with bridal party member

indicators.note: dancers move about, so the letters of the two words beside it are moved about

parts.note: taken letter for letter as fodder
taken letter for letter as fodder, joined by 'with'

explanation.surface: A late wedding guest arrives and takes to the dance floor with one of the bridesmaids.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridal party' looks like a wedding group, but 'party' belongs to the definition. The Liberal Democrats are a UK political party.
explanation.definitionFit: One who belongs to the Liberal Democrats, the centrist British political party, is a member of that party.

clue.text: Kind of question about personal skill?

definitions.meaning: split into three words it is what you ask when unsure you can do something

explanation.surface: A quiz setter wonders which sort of question tests someone's own talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind of question' reads as 'what type of question', but 'Kind' is an adjective standing alone; the rest is AM I ABLE, run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone friendly and good-natured is described as kind; both words mean pleasant towards others.

clue.text: Different parent blowing top

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the first letter, and blowing it means losing it

parts.note: one of a child's two parents

explanation.surface: A mum or dad losing their temper becomes a different person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blowing top' suggests an angry parent, but here it only removes the M at the head of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not the same as the thing already named is another, distinct one; an adjective of contrast.

clue.text: Vote against magazine slogan endorsing Trump over King

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something over flips it bottom to top

parts.note: a vote against is a no
the New Musical Express, a British music paper
Make America Great Again, his campaign slogan

explanation.surface: Voters reject a magazine that ran a pro-Trump slogan above a king.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'King' hides that it is the definition. NO, NME and MAGA are strung together, then the whole string is turned over.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend he was the ruler of Mycenae who led the Greek army against Troy, a famous monarch of myth.

clue.text: Describe as good-looking, now?

definitions.meaning: to set something out in words so it is understood
someone good-looking now is no longer plain: formerly plain

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to call a person handsome, at least these days.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as EX-PLAIN: 'ex' means former, so an ex-plain person was once plain and, the question mark suggests, is good-looking now.
explanation.definitionFit: To give an account of something so that others understand it is to set it out clearly in words.

clue.text: Grant for one in audio cut

indicators.note: audio is what is heard, so we want a sound rather than a spelling

parts.note: the actor Hugh Grant; 'for one' marks Hugh as one example of a Grant

explanation.surface: An actor's scene is trimmed from the soundtrack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' looks like an award or allowance; it is the first name of the actor Hugh Grant that is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: To chop wood or stone with an axe or blade is to hack or chop at it.

clue.text: Cover PM maintaining line in sand, shortly seizing old city church

indicators.note: to maintain something is to hold it, so the PM holds the line

parts.note: Edward Heath, British Prime Minister 1970-74
L is a standard abbreviation for line

indicators.note: to seize is to grab hold, so the shortened sand grabs the old city
cut short, so the word for sand loses its last letter

parts.note: used as it stands
sand loses its D
Ur of the Chaldees, the ancient Mesopotamian city
the Church of England

explanation.surface: A prime minister draws a line in the sand while a city church is taken over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line in sand' reads as a phrase but splits into three separate pieces, and 'old city church' likewise splits in two. Edward Heath was a Conservative prime minister of the 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: A policy paying medical bills is protection against illness costs, and cover is the insurer's term for protection.

clue.text: Did flatter grass outside hospital already save odd characters?

indicators.note: the word for grass sits outside the hospital, wrapping it

parts.note: slang for cannabis
H for hospital, as on road signs

indicators.note: save means except, so every letter of 'already' is kept apart from the odd-numbered ones

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of 'already'

explanation.surface: A patient flattered an informer outside hospital, trying to save something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' reads as an informer, flattered by someone; it is WEED wrapped round H. 'Odd characters' looks like strange people but means odd-numbered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Coaxing someone with sweet talk and compliments to get your way is the past tense of cajoling; a flatterer does it.

clue.text: Refuse to be knead-y?

definitions.meaning: the noun: waste, stressed on the first syllable
kneading is rubbing, and a joke adjective for being rather like it adds '-ish' to 'rub'

explanation.surface: Someone declines to be needy, spelled like a baker kneading dough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like the verb decline, and 'knead-y' plays on needy; it is the noun for waste plus RUB-ISH, 'somewhat rubbing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Household waste thrown away in bins is garbage or trash, which is what the noun refuse means.

clue.text: Resting tennis players getting energy shot they want

parts.note: the Association of Tennis Professionals, the men's tour
E for energy, as in physics
an unreturned serve, every tennis player's dream

explanation.surface: Tennis players taking a break get a boost from the serve they all hope to hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting' simply adds the next pieces on; 'they' in 'shot they want' points back to the tennis players.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying calm and still, or dead and buried, is to be tranquil or at rest, a gentle idiom.

clue.text: Work department cleaving to black pound

indicators.note: to cleave is to split, so the work department splits the words after it

parts.note: used as it stands
human resources
B for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: An office department sticks loyally to the black pound, the spending power of black consumers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleaving to' reads as clinging to, but cleave also means split, so the department splits the next two words apart. 'Pound' looks like money and is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A heart or a headache that beats heavily and rhythmically is pulsing, which is what pounding means here.

clue.text: Put off welcoming staff, keeling over and brought to life

indicators.note: a boat keeling over turns upside down, so the combined string is turned back to front
to welcome is to take in, so the word for 'put off' takes in the staff

parts.note: to discourage
a walking stick

explanation.surface: Workers are put off by welcoming new staff, who keel over and then are revived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees, but it is a walking stick; 'keeling over' applies to the whole combination, not just the staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A historical scene played out again by performers is made vivid and real, recreating it as live drama.

clue.text: Where Americans fought left-wing city about councillor

indicators.note: turning something about faces it the other way, so the whole string runs backwards

parts.note: short for Vietnam, the war's American nickname
red is the colour of the left
Los Angeles

explanation.surface: A history of a left-leaning city where Americans once fought, written about a councillor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Where Americans fought' tempts a battlefield like the Alamo; it is NAM, and the string NAM RED LA runs backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior member of a borough or city council, historically ranked above ordinary councillors, especially in London and the US.

clue.text: Sunak supporting a bad actor turned religious leader

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting means sitting underneath, so the Sunak piece comes last
turned round, so 'a bad actor' is read backwards

parts.note: a ham is an overacting performer
Rishi Sunak, British Prime Minister 2022-24

explanation.surface: A former prime minister backs a hammy actor who turns into a religious guru.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned religious leader' reads as a career change; 'turned' reverses A HAM, and the leader is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hindu title for a great sage or spiritual teacher, borne famously by the Beatles' guru, Maharishi Mahesh Yogi.

clue.text: Credulous one visiting part of church

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside a place, so 'one' goes inside the part of church

parts.note: the main body of a church, where the congregation sits
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A gullible tourist wanders into part of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Credulous one' looks like a noun phrase, but 'one' is the I that visits the church part.
explanation.definitionFit: Easily believing what one is told shows innocence and lack of worldly experience, so gullible.

clue.text: Spooner's excellent visitors in chat sites

indicators.note: Rev Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so his version swaps them here

parts.note: fab is slang for excellent, and takes the G from the next word
visitors are guests, and take the F from the word before

explanation.surface: Great guests turn up in online chat rooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chat sites' suggests websites; here it means gatherings where people chatter at length.
explanation.definitionFit: Long informal sessions of talking are occasions for gossip; gab is chatter and a fest is a gathering or festival.

clue.text: Bitter tree bark shunned by wooden boat

parts.note: the maple genus

indicators.note: to be shunned is to be left out, so the wooden boat is removed from the bark

parts.note: used as it stands
Noah's vessel, built of gopher wood

explanation.surface: Bitter tree bark is avoided by the builders of a wooden boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tree bark' reads as one thing, but it splits: the tree stands alone, and the bark is what the boat is taken from, leaving only B.
explanation.definitionFit: A sour, sharp taste or a harsh, cutting manner is acerbic; the shorter form is an older variant with the same sense.

clue.text: American uncle and captain reflected nation

indicators.note: a reflection shows things back to front, so the two names are read backwards

parts.note: Uncle Sam, the personification of the USA
the captain in Moby-Dick

explanation.surface: An American uncle and a ship's captain look back on their country.
explanation.walkthrough: SAM and AHAB are joined, then the whole of SAMAHAB is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An island country in the Atlantic off Florida, an independent state and Commonwealth member.

clue.text: Two questions initially avoided by milk and egg place?

indicators.note: the initial letters are avoided, so each question word loses its first letter

parts.note: two question words, when and who
to milk a situation is to exploit or use it

explanation.surface: Two questions about where milk and eggs come from are dodged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Milk and egg' reads like groceries; 'milk' is the verb USE, and 'egg place' is the definition. WHEN and WHO lose their Ws.
explanation.definitionFit: A coop where hens lay is where eggs come from; the question mark flags this playful description of a farm building.

clue.text: Lost red bats and grey one

indicators.note: bats is slang for crazy, so the letters beside it are scrambled

parts.note: fodder as it stands
fodder as it stands

explanation.surface: Red bats have gone missing, along with a grey one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' looks like the flying animals; it is the adjective for crazy, and 'grey one' is a person with grey hair.
explanation.definitionFit: An elderly person whose hair has gone silver with age is an old-timer, informally.

clue.text: Additionally skipping European backing tracks?

indicators.note: to skip something is to leave it out, so the European letter is dropped

parts.note: also, moreover
E for European

explanation.surface: Also leaving out European backing tracks from a playlist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing tracks' usually means accompaniment; here it is the tracks on the back of a single, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The secondary songs on the reverse of a vinyl single were on its flip side, literally at the back of the record.

clue.text: Sweet writer is thoughtless

parts.note: a fool is a British pudding of fruit folded into cream
Thomas Hardy, the novelist and poet

explanation.surface: A kindly author is careless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet writer' reads as a nice author; 'Sweet' is a dessert, a fool being a British fruit-and-cream pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: Recklessly bold, acting without considering risk, which is being careless and rash.

clue.text: Poet's earlier cut from "You there, boy!"

indicators.note: cutting something from a phrase removes it, leaving what is left

parts.note: the words run together. The same letters also run on unbroken across neighbouring clue words, a coincidence of the pieces sitting side by side; the setter gives no hidden-word signal.
ere is the poetic word for before

explanation.surface: A poet's earlier line is edited out of a call to a lad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poet's earlier' suggests an earlier poem; it is ERE, the poetic word for before, removed from the end of YOU THERE.
explanation.definitionFit: A young man or lad is called a youth; the word names a teenage male as well as the period of being young.

clue.text: Challenges of dead god

parts.note: D for dead, as in genealogies
the Greek god of war

explanation.surface: The trials set by a deity of the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead god' reads as one deity; it is D and ARES side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Provocations to do something risky are daring invitations, which is what a set of challenges can be.

clue.text: Claims Pippin, say, from sixteen players I forgot to mention

parts.note: a rugby scrum involves both packs of eight forwards
a postscript adds what the writer forgot

explanation.surface: Someone claims Pippin, the hobbit, came from a sixteen-strong team they forgot to mention.
explanation.walkthrough: Pippin looks like the hobbit; it is an apple variety, and to scrump is British slang for stealing apples from an orchard.
explanation.definitionFit: Helping oneself to a Pippin apple from someone's orchard without permission is taking fruit illicitly, a British slang verb.

clue.text: A Parisian, over barrel, deserted flat?

indicators.note: the French article is laid over the barrel, covering it on both sides

parts.note: French for 'a', feminine
a large cask for wine or beer
D is a recognised abbreviation for deserted

explanation.surface: A Parisian abandons a flat with a barrel in it.
explanation.walkthrough: UNE goes over TUN, then D is added. 'Flat' looks like an apartment, fitting 'deserted'; the question mark marks the musical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: An instrument off pitch sounds below the proper note, and a note sung or played too low is off-key.

clue.text: TV showing at least six games

definitions.meaning: in tennis a player must win six games to take one

explanation.surface: A television broadcasting half a dozen matches or more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'TV showing games' reads as a broadcast; the tennis sense is the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A television receiver is a set, and a tennis unit won by the first to six games, with a two-game lead, is one too.

clue.text: Article having fallen, these remains smashed?

definitions.text: Article having fallen, these remains smashed?

indicators.note: smashing breaks something into jumbled pieces, so the letters are scrambled
the article has fallen away, so it is dropped from what follows

parts.note: the indefinite article
fodder, which loses its A

explanation.surface: An object has fallen and all that remains is shattered.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, the whole clue describes the result: something falls and what is left lies smashed to tiny bits.
explanation.definitionFit: When an ornament falls and shatters, the tiny broken fragments left behind are what people call the bits.
